group: PSI Score: Pneumonia Severity Index for CAP
question:
Patient note:
An 82-year-old male who resides in a skilled nursing facility was brought to the emergency department this morning after several days of progressive shortness of breath, productive cough with rust-colored sputum, and subjective fevers noted by the facility staff on their overnight rounds. According to the transfer notes, he was last seen in his usual state of health four days earlier; since then he has refused two therapy sessions because of fatigue but has remained lucid, conversing normally with nurses and easily redirectable, without any reports of confusion or disorientation. Past medical history is significant for long-standing hypertension and stage 3b chronic kidney disease attributed to hypertensive nephrosclerosis; his most recent outpatient serum creatinine two months ago was 2.1 mg/dL with an estimated glomerular filtration rate in the mid-20s. He has no known history of stroke, transient ischemic attack, cirrhosis, or cancer, and he has never been diagnosed with congestive heart failure. He does not smoke and has not consumed alcohol for decades; all medications, including an ACE inhibitor, calcium-channel blocker, and low-dose aspirin, were taken as prescribed up until yesterday when oral intake began to wane because of malaise. Upon arrival he is seated upright on the stretcher, breathing rapidly but able to complete short sentences; he remains alert, answers questions appropriately, and names the month and location without difficulty. Initial vital signs prior to any interventions reveal an oral temperature of 39.1 °C, pulse 88 beats per minute with a regular rhythm, respiratory rate 28 breaths per minute, blood pressure 100/62 mm Hg, and oxygen saturation in the low 80s on room air, improving modestly with application of 2 L/min nasal cannula. Physical examination demonstrates flushed, warm skin; dry mucous membranes; and faint inspiratory crackles over the right lower lung field with dullness to percussion posteriorly. No jugular venous distention or peripheral edema is appreciated. Cardiac auscultation discloses a normal S1 and S2 without murmurs. Abdominal examination is benign, and there are no focal neurologic deficits. Point-of-care capillary glucose is 140 mg/dL. Laboratory studies drawn immediately, before the patient received fluids or antipyretics, show a hematocrit of 42 %, serum sodium 138 mEq/L, and blood urea nitrogen 30 mg/dL; creatinine is modestly above baseline at 2.3 mg/dL. Venous lactate is mildly elevated at 2.1 mmol/L. Arterial blood gas obtained on 2 L nasal cannula reveals pH 7.34, PaCO₂ 38 mm Hg, PaO₂ 55 mm Hg, and bicarbonate 20 mmol/L. Portable chest radiograph, reviewed at the bedside, demonstrates a consolidation in the right lower lobe with blunting of the right costophrenic angle suggestive of an accompanying small pleural effusion; no parenchymal abnormalities are seen on the contralateral side. Electrocardiogram shows normal sinus rhythm without ischemic changes. Urinalysis is bland aside from trace protein, consistent with his known kidney impairment. The nursing home director reports that influenza vaccination was administered this season, but pneumococcal vaccination status is uncertain. The patient denies recent hospitalization, exposure to sick contacts, or aspiration events. At this time he has not yet received antibiotics, intravenous fluids, or antipyretics; blood cultures, sputum culture, and nasopharyngeal swabs have been sent, and he is pending further diagnostic imaging to quantify the pleural fluid collection. The initial impression is community-acquired pneumonia involving the right lower lobe with an associated small effusion in an elderly gentleman with underlying chronic renal insufficiency and mild hypoxemia.

Question: What is the patient's Pneumonia Severity Index (PSI)? You should use the patient's medical values and health status when they were first admitted to the hospital prior to any treatment.
solution:
The Pneumonia Severity Index (PSI) sums demographic, comorbidity, examination, laboratory, and radiographic points at presentation.
- Demographics: male, age 82 → 82; skilled nursing facility residence → 10.
- Comorbidities: chronic renal disease → 10. No cancer, liver disease, heart failure, or cerebrovascular disease → 0 each.
- Examination: oriented → 0; respiratory rate 28 (<30/min) → 0; systolic BP 100 (not <90 mm Hg) → 0; temperature 39.1°C (neither <35 nor ≥40°C) → 0; pulse 88 (<125/min) → 0.
- Laboratory findings: arterial pH 7.34 (<7.35) → 30; BUN 30 (≥30 mg/dL) → 20; sodium 138 (not <130 mEq/L) → 0; glucose 140 (<250 mg/dL) → 0; hematocrit 42% (not <30%) → 0.
- Oxygenation: room-air saturation <90%, with PaO₂ 55 mm Hg even on oxygen → 10, counted once.
- Imaging: small pleural effusion → 10.
Sum: 82 + 10 + 10 + 30 + 20 + 10 + 10 = 172 (risk class V).
Final answer: 172
